description: Global projection of current energy system trends and the impact of stated policies.
pathwayDescription: The Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS) projects the energy sector’s current direction of travel, based on the latest market data, technology costs and in-depth analysis of the stated policies in countries around the world. STEPS provides a detailed projection of future outcomes based on current conditions, but does not attempt to predict which existing policies or economic conditions are more or less likely to change. The STEPS pathway corresponds to 2.4°C of warming by 2100 (50% probability). This is significantly higher than the IEA’s announced pledges scenario (APS), which projects 1.7°C of warming by 2100 (50% probability), and the IEA’s Net Zero scenario (NZE), which targets 1.5°C of warming by 2100 (50% probability).

coreDrivers.policies: The pathway models stated policies, such as energy subsisies or power development  plans, but does not include policy targets that lack specific provisions for their implementation. Carbon pricing is applied through existing and scheduled schemes, and target technology shares and capacity plans shape the power mix. Fossil fuel consumption subsidies are removed only where a specific commitment exists, and coal phase-out plans are carried where legislated or provisioned.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Unit technology costs are endogenous and deployment-linked: future cost evolution is tied to deployment levels, following a non-linear learning curve. Falling low-carbon capital costs drive build-out of solar and wind while coal and gas capital costs are held flat, so the relative economics shift toward low-carbon technologies, and utility-scale battery cost decreases which underpins the growth of storage capacity.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Low-carbon investment rises as a share of total energy investment. Average annual investment across supply, power and end-use grows from USD 3 254.8 billion in 2024-2030 to USD 3 653.0 billion in 2041-2050, while the fossil component (oil and gas supply, coal supply and unabated fossil generation) falls from USD 977.2 to USD 732.1 billion, so the fossil share drops from about 30% to about 20% and the low-carbon share rises correspondingly.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population follows the UN medium variant, reaching 9.68 billion in 2050, and GDP grows from USD 175,981 billion to USD 357,510 billion (2023, PPP).

dependencies.dependency_description: Policy support is the organising assumption of this pathway but is not stretched beyond what is already in place or provisioned, so it enables the decarbonisation levers without being a binding condition on them. Carbon pricing covers only the jurisdictions that already have schemes, efficiency and vehicle standards pull end-use electrification along, and renewable and capacity targets shape the power mix.

Permitting and grid planning rules set the pace at which the electrification lever can be delivered, without being the dominant constraint at this pathway's deployment rate. Grid projects can take over a decade to complete, much longer than the renewable projects they serve, and connection queues and congestion have already arisen from delayed extensions. Global grid line length grows about 15% by 2030.

Cost of capital and carbon prices shape which levers are economic, but the pathway does not require market conditions to change. Financing costs differ by technology and by stage of economic development which favours variable renewables over firm low-carbon capacity in exactly the regions that need capacity most. Carbon prices exist only where already scheduled, so in most of the world the hydrogen and CCUS levers have no price signal and stay small.

The only acceptance risk the publication names is local opposition to proposed transmission line routes, cited as one of several complications in grid project delivery. That matters for the electrification lever, since grid expansion is its precondition, but at this pathway's build rate the exposure is correspondingly limited. No acceptance issue is raised for generation technologies.

End-use electrification is the largest lever in this pathway and it runs through household and firm purchasing decisions, so adoption rates are a real constraint on it. This is driven by regulation and falling production costs rather than by preference, and flags that public charging availability remains a major hurdle in rural areas, where long-distance driving is common and long heat pump payback periods of ten to 13 years.

The electrification lever depends on grid and storage build-out that is already constrained. Global grid line length grows about 15% by 2030; network investment nearly doubles by 2050 from current levels and battery investment rises, raising storage capacity. Grid projects take over a decade against much shorter renewable project timelines, which has already produced connection queues and congestion.

The pathway depends on emerging technologies only modestly. Captured CO2 reaches 395 Mt and DAC 44 Mt by 2050, low-emissions hydrogen production 4.7 EJ, DAC and hydrogen are present but immaterial to the outcome. Battery storage is the exception and is the one new technology this pathway genuinely relies on. Costs are endogenous and deployment-linked.

The publication warns that reduced investment following the 2023 price fall could cause future supply shortages and price spikes for critical minerals, which would slow or reverse clean energy cost reductions. Concentration risk compounds it, with tariffs and trade measures narrowing supply routes for solar PV, EVs and batteries. Land availability is not assessed anywhere, and bioenergy demand reaches 56.1 EJ of modern solid bioenergy supply without any stated land constraint.

The publication raises physical climate risk to energy infrastructure from extreme weather as a general concern and identifies it among the risks to fuel supply chains, but it models no climate impact on any decarbonisation lever and quantifies no adaptation requirement.

Over 6 million additional energy workers are needed worldwide by 2030, and the publication states that several parts of the energy industry already face skill shortages, with clean energy sectors competing for the same limited pool of construction workers, welders and electricians - the same trades the grid build-out depends on, where a shortage of qualified staff is already named as a cause of project delay.
